# DATA-3 results — generated by `run_supply.py`, not hand-edited

4 end products, 32 sub-assemblies, **260 purchased parts**, 442 BOM lines, 50 suppliers (68 single-sourced parts), 390 open POs and 3624 received POs of history. Horizon: **13 weeks**.

Why 13 weeks: it covers most purchased-part lead times plus a planning cycle, so an order placed today still lands inside the window. Beyond it, forecast uncertainty starts to dominate supply uncertainty and the analysis is answering a sales question wearing a materials hat.

This is the artifact that changes the materials meeting. "P50 says 120" invites a commitment; "P10 84, P50 120, P90 140, and the gating part is PRT-0041 from a single source" invites a decision. A point estimate on a supply plan is a forecast pretending to be a fact.

### Is the fan calibrated?

| product | % of simulations below the P50 | % inside P10–P90 |
|---|---|---|
| PRD-A | 12.8% | 97.1% |
| PRD-B | 0.0% | 97.5% |
| PRD-C | 2.0% | 98.7% |
| PRD-D | 17.6% | 95.5% |

These should be near 50% and 80%. They are *self-consistency* checks — the percentiles are computed from the same simulations they are scored against, so this verifies the arithmetic, not the model. Deviations come from discreteness (buildable units are integers, so many simulations tie exactly at the percentile). **Genuine calibration would require comparing the fan against realised outcomes, which needs a simulated future this project does not run** — that is named in the README as not built.

## 3. Shortage drivers, with order-by dates

| part | supplier | single source | times gating | first impact | lead mean | lead P95 | **order by (day)** | too late? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PRT-0146 | SUP-038 | no | 2654 | week 6 | 43 d | 52 d | **day -10** | **ALREADY LATE** |
| PRT-0100 | SUP-038 | no | 1895 | week 9 | 43 d | 52 d | **day +11** | no |
| PRT-0008 | SUP-034 | no | 1676 | week 8 | 37 d | 51 d | **day +5** | no |
| PRT-0109 | SUP-043 | no | 1227 | week 3 | 61 d | 84 d | **day -63** | **ALREADY LATE** |
| PRT-0177 | SUP-016 | **yes** | 1056 | week 8 | 46 d | 67 d | **day -11** | **ALREADY LATE** |
| PRT-0200 | SUP-032 | no | 978 | week 10 | 27 d | 46 d | **day +24** | no |
| PRT-0062 | SUP-031 | no | 642 | week 3 | 69 d | 89 d | **day -68** | **ALREADY LATE** |
| PRT-S021 | SUP-049 | no | 573 | week 4 | 45 d | 64 d | **day -36** | **ALREADY LATE** |
| PRT-0027 | SUP-030 | no | 174 | — | 60 d | 93 d | **day -2** | **ALREADY LATE** |
| PRT-0192 | SUP-050 | no | 159 | — | 23 d | 37 d | **day +54** | no |

6 of 10 top drivers are **already past their order-by date** — the runway was consumed before anyone looked.

The order-by date is computed from the **P95** lead time, not the mean. Ordering a gating part to its mean lead time means arriving late half the time, which for the part that stops the line is not a plan. That single substitution is the difference between an alert that is a fact ("you will be short in week 7") and an alert that is a decision ("order by day −3 or the line stops in week 7").

## 4. Supplier deterioration — caught by distributions, not averages

Planted disruptions: 6. Flagged: 7. **Precision 0.43, recall 0.50.**

| disruption type | planted | caught | caught by the P95 trigger alone |
|---|---|---|---|
| lead_time_doubling | 3 | 1 | 0 |
| tail_blowout | 3 | 2 | 1 |

The `tail_blowout` row is the argument for watching distributions. Those suppliers have a mean lead time that has barely moved and a P95 that has doubled — they are the ones that will stop a line, and every mean-based monitor and every OTD percentage says they are fine. The P95 and variance triggers are what catch them.

**The `lead_time_doubling` row is a poor result and is not dressed up: 1 of 3 caught.** These should be the EASY ones — the mean itself moves. They are missed because the detector compares a 120-day recent window against a 245-day baseline on ~15 receipts per supplier, and with that few points a doubled mean does not always clear a 1.25x ratio threshold against a noisy baseline. The fix is not a cleverer statistic, it is more history per supplier-part or a sequential test (CUSUM on lead time) that accumulates evidence instead of comparing two windows — DATA-2 in this portfolio has the machinery and the two are not wired together.

At precision 0.43 this raises roughly one false alarm per true one. In a weekly materials review that may be acceptable — a flagged supplier costs a phone call — but it is a real operating point and it is reported rather than tuned until it looked good. A threshold sweep to characterise the tradeoff properly is not built.

| supplier | mean ratio | P95 ratio | sd ratio | triggers |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUP-044 | 1.22× | 2.09× | 3.19× | p95, variance |
| SUP-027 | 1.41× | 1.86× | 2.41× | mean, p95, variance |
| SUP-011 | 1.77× | 1.74× | 2.11× | mean, p95, variance |

## 5. OTIF, and the definitional trap

On-time-in-full against **which** promise: the original one made when the order was placed, or the latest agreed reschedule?

| supplier | receipts | OTIF vs original | OTIF vs latest promise | gap (pts) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SUP-036 | 28 | 35.7% | 100.0% | **+64.3** |
| SUP-009 | 26 | 38.5% | 100.0% | **+61.5** |
| SUP-003 | 70 | 42.9% | 100.0% | **+57.1** |
| SUP-006 | 42 | 42.9% | 100.0% | **+57.1** |
| SUP-021 | 72 | 43.1% | 100.0% | **+56.9** |
| SUP-048 | 112 | 43.8% | 100.0% | **+56.2** |
| SUP-018 | 102 | 44.1% | 100.0% | **+55.9** |
| SUP-045 | 68 | 44.1% | 100.0% | **+55.9** |
| SUP-024 | 49 | 44.9% | 100.0% | **+55.1** |
| SUP-042 | 109 | 45.9% | 100.0% | **+54.1** |

Against the latest reschedule, a supplier who is chronically late but always calls ahead scores near 100%. That is the number suppliers prefer and it is the ERP default in a lot of configurations, because the promise field gets overwritten in place. **The scorecard here uses the ORIGINAL promise**, and reports the gap as its own metric — a direct measure of how much a supplier is managing their score rather than their delivery.

The weights are printed and the score decomposes into contributions, because the first question a sourcing manager asks is "why is this supplier red" — and a composite with hidden weights is an opinion wearing a number's clothes.

## 7. Allocation policy when a shared component is short

| policy | total P50 units | worst product fill rate | PRD-A | PRD-B | PRD-C | PRD-D |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| even | 620 | 19.6% | 30.6% | 19.6% | 21.3% | 31.1% |
| margin | 630 | 19.6% | 30.2% | 19.6% | 24.5% | 29.7% |
| contract | 629 | 19.6% | 30.1% | 19.6% | 24.5% | 29.7% |

Shared components are where the shortage maths gets interesting, because someone has to decide who gets the part. That is a business policy, not an arithmetic fact, and the three policies produce different plans and different angry people. The job of the analysis is to make the tradeoff explicit and quantified — not to pick.
